args.text: [lane-lynx] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, which turns site names into addresses) answers for too long: (1) Stale answers: users are sent to an old address after a server moves, so the service looks down. (2) Slow recovery: if a site fails over to a backup, cached entries keep sending people to the broken one. (3) Lingering bad data: a poisoned or wrong answer stays in the cache longer, so harm lasts longer and is harder to undo.

[lane-lynx] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave a sender unsure whether a request worked, so it must be able to try again. If repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicate order.

[lane-lynx] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier that starts with a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, larger than a standard 4 or 8 byte integer, so indexes grow bigger. (2) Leaked timing: the embedded timestamp reveals when a record was created, which may be unwanted, and ordering within the same millisecond is not guaranteed.

[lane-lynx] A write-ahead log is a record where a database saves each change to durable storage before applying it to its main data files. After a crash, the database replays this log to recover committed work and discard unfinished changes, so no confirmed data is lost.

[lane-lynx] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: an automatic update could change speed or behaviour between runs, so differences in results might come from the client rather than the thing being tested. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the same setup later and get comparable results, and any change in numbers can be traced to a deliberate edit.

[lane-lynx] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal to producers that it is full or falling behind, so they slow down, wait or are refused instead of piling on more work. This keeps memory use and delays under control and stops a slow consumer from causing a wider failure.

[lane-lynx] Two ways a cron (timed job scheduler) job can run twice: (1) Overlap: a run takes longer than the gap between runs, so the next starts while the first is still going. (2) Duplicate hosts: the same schedule is installed on more than one server, so each fires it. One guard: take a lock, such as a lock file or database lock, at the start and exit if it is already held.

[lane-lynx] A tombstone is a marker written in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. It lets every copy learn about the deletion, so a copy that missed it cannot bring the old value back. Tombstones are removed only after a set time, once all copies have had a chance to see them.

[lane-lynx] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than truly failing: (1) Mixed results on identical code: it passes on some runs and fails on others without any change to the code or inputs. (2) Timing or order dependence: it fails only under load, on certain machines, or when run after particular other tests, and passes when run alone.

[lane-lynx] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock for a fixed time, and each side judges that time using its own clock. If the holder's clock runs slow or the lock service's clock runs fast, the holder believes it still has the lock after the service has given it to someone else. Two parties then act as owner at once, which defeats the lock.

[lane-lynx] Two costs of very long feature branches: (1) Painful merges: the longer a branch lives, the further it drifts from the main line, so combining them brings many clashes that take time to fix. (2) Late feedback: reviewers and testers see a huge change all at once, so problems are found late and are harder to review and to undo.

[lane-lynx] A canary release sends a new version to a small share of real users first and checks whether it behaves as well as the current one, looking at errors, speed and resource use. If the signs are healthy the release widens step by step, and if not it is pulled back before most users are affected.

[lane-lynx] Two risks of keeping secrets in environment variables: (1) they leak easily, because they can show up in crash reports, logs, debugging output or process listings, and child programs inherit them by default; (2) they are hard to control, since there is no built-in access check, audit trail or easy way to rotate them without restarting the program.

[lane-lynx] P50 latency (the 50th percentile, or median) is the response time that half of all requests beat, so it shows the typical experience. P99 latency is the time that 99 in every 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that a small share of users still meet. A service can have a fine p50 and a poor p99, which is why both are watched.

[lane-lynx] Two reasons a cache hit rate can drop after a deploy: (1) The cache keys changed, for example a new version prefix or a different key format, so old stored entries no longer match and every request misses until the cache warms up again. (2) The cache was emptied or the servers restarted, so a cold cache starts with nothing stored; new servers also begin cold. Changed expiry settings can add to this.

[lane-lynx] Head-of-line blocking happens when items wait in a strict single-file queue and the first item is slow or stuck, so everything behind it must wait too, even if those items are quick or ready. Examples: one lost packet holding up later data on a single connection, or one slow request delaying others in the same queue. Separate queues or parallel connections reduce it.
